questions.question: Which broad area takes the largest share of UK public spending?

options.B: Social protection, including pensions and benefits

questions.why: HM Treasury PESA consistently shows social protection as the largest function of public spending, ahead of health.

questions.question: Spending on a service rose after inflation, but its share of total spending fell. How is that possible?

options.A: It is not possible; one figure must be wrong
options.B: Total spending grew faster than spending on that service
options.D: The service was moved to local councils

questions.why: A share depends on the total, so real spending on one area can rise while its share falls if the total rises faster.

questions.question: In recent decades, UK public spending has roughly equalled what share of national income (GDP)?
questions.why: OBR and ONS figures put total managed expenditure at roughly 40-45% of GDP in most recent years.

questions.question: Health spending rose from one cash amount to a higher one over 20 years. What does that alone tell you?

options.C: Spending rose in pounds, but not whether it rose after inflation

questions.why: Cash figures must be adjusted for inflation (real terms) before you can say real resources rose.

questions.question: Which single tax raises the most money for the UK government?
questions.why: HMRC receipts show income tax is the largest single source of tax revenue.

questions.question: When public spending is higher than all taxes and other receipts, how is the gap mainly covered?

options.A: Printing a new tax each year

questions.why: The gap is public sector net borrowing, which is not a tax or a receipt.

questions.question: Government receives interest and dividends on assets it owns. How do official statistics classify that money?
questions.why: ONS and OBR count interest and dividends as receipts that are not taxes, distinct from both taxes and borrowing.

questions.question: Which tax is set and collected by local councils rather than HMRC?
questions.why: Council tax is a local tax that councils set and collect to fund local services.

questions.question: Roughly what share of all income tax is paid by the top 1% of income taxpayers?

options.C: Around a quarter to under a third

questions.why: HMRC income tax liabilities statistics have put the top 1% share at roughly 25-30% for many years.

questions.question: Which income group pays the highest share of its disposable income in indirect taxes like VAT and duties?

options.D: All groups pay exactly the same share

questions.why: ONS Effects of taxes and benefits shows indirect taxes take the largest share of disposable income for the poorest fifth.

questions.question: If the top 1% pay about 28% of all income tax, what does 28% describe?

options.B: Their share of total income tax revenue
options.C: The share of their household income spent on tax
options.D: The share of adults in the top 1%

questions.why: A share of total revenue is different from a personal tax rate or a household's tax as a share of income.

questions.question: Someone earns too little to pay income tax. Do they still contribute tax?

options.A: No, they pay no tax at all
options.B: Yes, through indirect taxes such as VAT on purchases
options.C: Only if they own a company

questions.why: VAT and duties are paid on spending by almost everyone, regardless of income tax status.

questions.question: In ONS household tax statistics, which of these is an indirect tax?
questions.why: ONS counts VAT and duties as indirect taxes; income tax, employee NICs and council tax are direct.

questions.question: In household tax statistics, what does 'combined' or 'total' taxes mean?
questions.why: ONS sums direct and indirect taxes to give total taxes paid by households.

questions.question: An average household in a group pays about a third of gross income in tax. What does this mean?

options.A: Everyone in the group pays a 33% income tax rate
options.B: The group pays a third of all UK tax
options.C: On average, total taxes equal about a third of the group's gross income
options.D: A third of the group pays tax

questions.why: A household average share of income is neither a personal tax rate nor a share of national tax revenue.

questions.question: A page shows a clearly labelled example family and its tax bill. How should you treat it?

options.B: As an illustration, separate from measured statistics
options.C: As the tax every family pays
options.D: As a forecast of next year

questions.why: Example households are illustrations built on assumptions, not measured figures for real households.

questions.question: The UK headline employment rate measures what?

options.B: The share of people aged 16 to 64 who are in work
options.C: The share of workers in full-time jobs
options.D: The share of people claiming no benefits

questions.why: ONS's headline employment rate is the proportion of people aged 16 to 64 in employment, from the Labour Force Survey.

questions.question: Average pay rose 5% in a year while prices rose 7%. What happened to real pay?
questions.why: Real pay growth is roughly cash pay growth minus inflation, so 5% minus 7% is about minus 2%.

questions.question: What is the most common housing tenure in England?
questions.why: The English Housing Survey shows around two thirds of households own their home.

questions.question: Which country do UK residents visit most often on trips abroad?
questions.why: ONS Travel trends has shown Spain as the top destination for UK residents' visits abroad for many years.

questions.question: In England, what is the legal limit for infant classes (ages 5 to 7) with one teacher?
questions.why: The School Admissions (Infant Class Sizes) regulations cap infant classes in England at 30 per qualified teacher.

questions.question: A survey was not carried out in 2020. How should a year-by-year chart show 2020?

options.C: As a clearly marked gap with no data

questions.why: Missing years must be shown as missing, not filled with zero or silently interpolated.

questions.question: Employment rose in the years after a new policy began. What can you conclude from that alone?

options.C: Employment rose, but this does not show the policy caused it

questions.why: A change over time does not by itself establish cause; other factors may explain it.

questions.question: Why should a class size figure say which nation and school phase it covers?

options.A: It does not matter; all UK figures are identical
options.B: Nations collect data differently and primary and secondary classes differ

questions.why: Education is devolved, so definitions and collections differ by nation, and class sizes differ by phase.
